1. The present accident claim is based on a detailed accident report (Dar) filed by the police in
terms of provisions of Mv Act. 
2.  As per the investigation by the police officials, on 19.04.2019, Constable Mahabir informed through call vide DD no. 038 about an accident on South Extension Ring Road. Police officials reached the spot and found one car and a pedal rickshaw in an accidental condition and injured rickshaw puller was removed to the hospital. An FIR 0136/2019 was registered u/s 279/337 of IPC and upon investigation charge sheet was filed against driver /respondent no. 1 u/s 279/338 of IPC. 
Present DAR was also filed by the investigating officer. 
As per record, constable Mahabir had witnessed the accident and claimed that respondent no.1 while driving his car no. DL 3CAZ 7186 (hereinafter referred as the offending vehicle) MACT No.
677/19 Binod Das vs. Devansh Gupta Page no. 2 of 21 BK in a rash and negligent manner, had hit the petitioner who was plying his rickshaw. The offending vehicle is claimed to be owned by respondent no.2 and insured with respondent no. 3. 
During trial of the case, petitioner expired and the claim was pursued by his legal heirs including the wife and 3 minor children of the deceased. 
3. Respondents have filed their reply wherein Respondent no. 1 and 2 have denied the accident to have taken place due to negligence of respondent no.1. It has been pleaded that the petitioner himself blatantly violated the traffic rules and was pulling his rickshaw on the wrong side of the road and that the accident occurred due to the sole negligence of such petitioner. As per reply of Respondent no.3, cause of action does not survive as the petitioner has now expired. It is further pleaded that the legal heirs of the petitioner are not entitled to any compensation unless the accident resulted in death of the petitioner. 
4. From the pleadings of parties, the following issues were framed on 13.12.2019. 
1. Whether the injured suffered injuries in a road traffic accident on 19.04.2019 due to rash and negligent driving of vehicle no. DL 3CAZ 7186 being driven by R1, owned by R2 and insured with R3? OPP 2. Whether the petitioner is entitled to any compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom?

Sh. Rajender Singh, record clerk AIIMS Trauma Center was examined as PW-2. He produced complete treatment record of patient /petitioner Binod Das as Ex.PW2/1. He was cross examined by Ld. Counsel for respondents. 
Dr. Srikanth, SR (Emergency Medicine) JPN Truama Center, AIIMS was examined ad PW-3. He deposed that based on the discharge summery of the patient, the patient had suffered traumatic brain injury and that at the time of his discharge, he was not in complete control of mental faculties. 
He was duly cross examined by Ld. Counsel for respondents. 
HC Mahavir was examined as PW-4. He deposed that he was eye witness to this accident and relied upon FIR no. 136/2019 as Ex.PW4/1. He was duly cross examined by Ld. Counsel for respondents. 
6. No evidence was led on behalf of respondents. 
7. Arguments were addressed by counsels for petitioner as well as respondent. 
8. On the basis of material on record, evidence adduced and arguments addressed, issue wise findings are as under :-

In Bimla Devi & Ors vs. Himachal Road Transport Corporation & ors [(2009) 13 SC 530,[ in Kaushnumma Begum and others v/s New India Assurance Company Limited, [2001 ACJ 421 SC[, in National Insurance Co. Ltd. vs. Pushpa Rana cited as [2009 ACJ 287], it has been held that the negligence has to be decided on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities and a holistic view is to be taken. It has been further held that the proceedings under the Motor Vehicle Act are not akin to the proceedings in a Civil Suit and hence, strict rules of evidence are not applicable.
10. In the present case, police after investigation had filed charge-sheet against respondent no.1 under section 279/338 IPC which is also suggestive of negligence of respondent in causing the accident. The IO has filed Detailed Accident Report before this Tribunal. In National Insurance Co.

3 Vs. Pushpa Rana 2009 ACJ 287 Delhi , it was laid down that completion of investigation and filing of chargesheet are sufficient proof of negligence of the driver of the offending vehicle. 
11. It may further be noted that including in the case of Cholamandlam insurance company Ltd. Vs.
Kamlesh 2009 (3) AD Delhi 310, it is held by Hon'ble Supreme Court/ Hon'ble High Court that if driver of offending vehicle does not enter the witness box, an adverse inference can be drawn against him. 
12. In the present case also, driver did not enter into the MACT No. 677/19 Binod Das vs. Devansh Gupta Page no. 5 of 21 BK witness box to controvert the claim of petitioner or even to explain circumstances of accident. 
13. On perusal of examination-in-chief by way of affidavit of PW-1, it is noted that PW-1/Petitioner deposed on the lines of petitioner's original stand as already noted above. It was further deposed that due to rash and negligent driving of the R-1, the accident in question took place.
14. Such witness was cross-examined by learned counsel for insurance company/R-3. She averred that she is not the eye witness to the accident and at the time of accident, she was in her hometown. 
Her parents-in-law were pre-deceased before the death of injured. She deposed that injured(now deceased) was rickshaw puller. Injured was discharged on 05.05.2019. Injured had not taken any treatment from anywhere than AIIMS. She also admitted in cross that her husband(injured, now deceased) died as he fell from Barapullah flyover due to his mental health. She told that her deceased husband was earning Rs.18,000/-p.m. She denied the suggestion that her husband did not die due to accidental injury but died due to some independent reason. 
She was also cross-examined by Ld. Counsel for R-1&R-2 in which admitted that she is not an eye witness and cannot say whether driver of offending vehicle was driving the vehicle in rash and negligent manner.
15. PW-2 Sh. Rajender Singh was a summoned witness from AIIMS trauma center. He proved the complete medical record of injured (now deceased) as Ex.PW-2/1(colly). In his cross- examination,
he admitted. He admitted that name mentioned in MLC was "unknown" but his age and religion was mentioned.

He deposed that as per medical documents, injured (now deceased) has severe traumatic brain injury and at the time of discharge, he was not in complete control of mental faculties. He was cross-examined by learned counsel for insurance company, he admitted that he is not a specialist in Neuro department. He was also cross-examined by learned counsel for R-1&R-2 where he denied the suggestion that patient was in complete control of mental faculties as per discharge documents.

He told that accident took place at around 1.30 pm and injured(now deceased) was plying rickshaw at the time of accident and offending vehicle hit it from behind, again he said that from which side, it hit the rickshaw, he does know. He denied the suggestion that he was not an eye witness to the accident. He pulled the rickshaw and car to the side of the road. He denied the suggestion that rickshaw puller was plying on wrong side or that negligence was on the part of him. He denied the suggestion that driver of Wagon-R was not negligent or at high speed. 
18. Further no evidence to contrary led by any of the respondent including by the R-1/driver. 
Despite the fact that in his reply, R-1 &2 claimed that petitioner himself was negligent and violating the traffic rules and driving on wrong side of the MACT No. 677/19 Binod Das vs. Devansh Gupta Page no. 7 of 21 BK road. Thus, it is held that respondent no.1 &2 totally failed to prove their defence. 
19. Before parting with the issue, it is pertinent to mention that though the issue framed pertains only to the injury suffered by the petitioner (since deceased) during evidence, it was claimed that the petitioner subsequently died due to such accident. It is claimed that owing to the head injury,
petitioner suffered from serious neurological issues and once left the house and jumped of the flyover resulting in his death. However, there is no assessment of the neurological disability on record nor the petitioner's kin have been able to establish any nexus between the injury suffered in the accident and subsequent death of the petitioner. Bald aversion as these cannot be entertained without a legal basis or documentary proof. It may further be noted that in present case, even the medical treatment paper also support the nature of injury and that it is result of road accident, but the subsequent death of such injured is not correlated with the accident. Considering the period of hospitalization and MLC, the injury is assessed to be grievous in nature. 
20. In fact, factum of such accident, involvement of R-1 vehicle is not in dispute in present case but the only dispute is whether it is due to rash and negligent driving of R-1 that the accident in question took place. 
21. As such, in view of the material on record, evidence proved on record, charge-sheet against respondent and that respondent no.1/driver did not enter into witness box, the issue No.1 is decided accordingly, in favour of the petitioner. 
Contributory Negligence MACT No. 677/19 Binod Das vs. Devansh Gupta Page no. 8 of 21 BK 22. It may be noted that in present case, a defence of contributory negligence is taken. As already noted above, Ld counsel for Respondent has argued that it is the victim who was plying his rickshaw in the wrong direction and therefore, however, no evidence has been led by Respondents to prove that such petitioner was plying his rickshaw in a direction violating the traffic norms. Even if so,
there is no plea that such rickshaw suddenly appeared from a wrong directions which could not have been foreseen. Hence, with no evidence to prove contributory negligence on part of petitioner, the Binod Das vs Devansh Gupta (136/19Kmp) on 9 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/36038976/
5 defence is held unsustainable. 
Issue no. 2 Whether the petitioner is entitled to any compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom? OPP 23. At this stage, before proceeding further, by rely upon the judgments of C.K. Subramania Iyer v.
T. Kunhikuttan Nair, R.D. Hattangadi v. Pest Control (India) (P) Ltd. and Baker v. Willoughby which are referred and relied in Raj Kumar Vs. Ajay Kumar & Anr. (2011) 1 Supreme Court cases 343 decided by Hon'ble SC, it can be noted that the provision of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 ("the Act", for short) makes it clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation should,
to the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the accident. 
The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner. The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess MACT No. 677/19 Binod Das vs. Devansh Gupta Page no. 9 of 21 BK the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable. A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury. This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned. 
24. Further it can be noted that the heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:
Pecuniary damages (Special damages)
(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalisation, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure.
(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment;
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability.
(iii) Future medical expenses. 
Non-pecuniary damages (General damages)
(iv) Damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries. 
(v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage).

6 (vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity).
24.1. In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under heads (i), (ii) (a)
and (iv). 24.2. It is only in serious cases of injury, where there is specific MACT No. 677/19 Binod Das vs. Devansh Gupta Page no. 10 of 21 BK medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii)(b), (iii),
(v) and (vi) relating to loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability, future medical expenses, loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage) and loss of expectation of life.
24.3. Assessment of pecuniary damages under Item (i) and under Item (ii) (a) do not pose much difficulty as they involve reimbursement of actuals and are easily ascertainable from the evidence.
24.4. Award under the head of future medical expenses--Item (iii)--depends upon specific medical evidence regarding need for further treatment and cost thereof. 
24.5. Assessment of non-pecuniary damages--Items (iv), (v) and (vi)--involves determination of l u m p s u m a m o u n t s w i t h r e f e r e n c e t o c i r c u m s t a n c e s s u c h a s a g e , n a t u r e o f injury/deprivation/disability suffered by the claimant and the effect thereof on the future life of the claimant. Decisions of Hon'ble SC and Hon'ble High Courts contain necessary guidelines for award under these heads, if necessary. 24.6. It was observed by Hon'ble Sc in such case of Raj Kumar (supra) that what usually poses some difficulty is the assessment of the loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability--Item (ii) (a).
24.7. We are not concerned with assessment regarding loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability in this case, as petitioner did not suffer any permanent disability.
25. PW-1/ Smt. Sajan Devi, wife of injured deposed that she MACT No. 677/19 Binod Das vs.
Devansh Gupta Page no. 11 of 21 BK and her minor sons namely Raju Kumar, Pavan Kumar and Radhi Kumari are legal heirs of the injured Binod Das(now deceased). Accident was occurred on 19.04.2019 and injured(now deceased) remained admitted from 19.04.2019 to 05.05.2019 and operated twice. Due to head injury, his mental condition became worst and he used to behave like mad person. On 30.07.2019, he left home and she came to know that injured fell from Barapulla flyover due to his mental illness. Injured(now deceased) was a rickshaw puller in Delhi and used to earn Rs.18,000/- per month. 
26. During cross examination of such witness by insurance company, nothing material to the contrary could be extracted by the respondent side. 
27. Thus, on the basis of evidence proved on record, it is held that injured was a rickshaw puller, his income as per Minimum Wages Act for unskilled labour,Delhi is taken as Rs.14,000/- p.m. It is further held that due to such injuries, he could be able to work for 3 months.

A claim to loss of estate, including expenditure on medicines, treatment, diet, attendant, doctor's fee etc. would however be maintainable.

Ltd., MAC Appeal no. 433/2013, decided on 18.10.2022 it was noted regarding rate of interest:
"25 to evaluate the submission made by counsel for the applicants, it is imperative to examine the guiding principles for the grant of interest. In Abati Bezbaruah Vs.
Binod Das vs Devansh Gupta (136/19Kmp) on 9 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/36038976/
9 Geological Survey of India, (2003) 3 SCC 148, the following was held while interpreting section 171 of the MV Act, 1988:-
Three decisions were cited before us by Mr. A. P. Mohanty, learned counsel appearing on behalf of the Appellant, in support of his contentions. No ratio has been laid down in any of the decisions in regard to the rate of interest and the rate of interest was awarded on the amount of compensation as a matter of judicial discretion. The rate of interest must be just and reasonable depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case and taking all relevant factors including inflation, change of economy,
policy being adopted by Reserve Bank of India from time to time, how long the case is pending, permanent injuries suffered by the victim, enormity of suffering, loss of future income, loss of enjoyment of life etc. into consideration. No rate of interest is fixed under Section 171 of the MV Act 1988. Varying rates of interest are being awarded by Tribunals, High Courts and the Supreme Court. Interest can be granted even if a claimant does not specifically plead for the same as it is consequential in the eye of the law. Interest is compensation for forbearance or detention of money and that interest being awarded to a party only for being kept out of the money which ought to have been paid to him. No principle could be deduced nor can any rate of interest be fixed to have a general application in motor accident provision under Section 171 giving discretion to the Tribunal in such matter. In other matters,
awarding of interest depends upon the statutory provisions mercantile usage and doctrine of equity. Neither Sec. 34 CPC nor Sec. 4-A(3) of Workmen's Compensation Act are applicable in the matter of fixing are of interest in a claim under the Motor Vehicles Act. 
MACT No. 677/19 Binod Das vs. Devansh Gupta Page no. 15 of 21 BK The courts have awarded the interest at different rates depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case. Therefore, in my opinion, there cannot be any hard and fast rule in awarding interest and the award of interest is solely on the discretion of the Tribunal of the High Court as indicated above."
31. Having regard to the prevailing rate of interest and the judgments of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India, including in the case of Erudhaya Priya vs State Express Transport decided on 27 July, 2020,
Civil Appeal Nos. 2811-2812 OF 2020 [Arising out of SLP (C) Nos.8495-8496 of 2018], which is three Judges Bench judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court, such interest @ 9% per annum is deemed fit and accordingly granted in the present case.

37. At this stage, it is relevant to the refer to the judgment of A. V. Padma & Ors. Vs., R. Venugopal &
Ors. (2012) 3 Supreme Court Cases 378:
" ......In the case of Susamma Thomas (supra), this Court issued certain guidelines in order to "safeguard the feed from being frittered away by the beneficiaries due to ignorance, illiteracy and susceptibility to exploitation". 
Even as per the guidelines issued by this Court Court, long term fixed deposit of amount of compensation is mandatory only in the case of minors, illiterate claimants and widows. In the case of MACT No. 677/19 Binod Das vs. Devansh Gupta Page no. 17 of 21 BK illiterate claimants, the Tribunal is allowed to consider the request for lumpsum payment for effecting purchase of any movable property such as agricultural implements, rickshaws etc. to earn a living. However, in such cases, the Tribunal shall make sure that the amount is actually spent for the purpose and the demand is not a ruse to withdraw money. In the case of semi-illiterate claimants, the Tribunal should ordinarily invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit. But if the Tribunal is satisfied for reasons to be stated in writing that the whole or part of the amount is required for expanding an existing business or for purchasing some property for earning a livelihood, the Tribunal can release the whole or part of the amount of compensation to the claimant provided the Tribunal will ensure that the amount is invested for the purpose for which it is demanded and paid. 
In the case of literate persons, it is not mandatory to invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit.

11 The expression used in guideline No. (iv) issued by this Court is that in the case of literate persons also the Tribunal may resort to the procedure indicated in guideline No. (i), whereas in the guideline Nos. (i), (ii), (iii) and (v), the expression used is that the Tribunal should. Moreover, in the case of literate persons, the Tribunal may resort to the procedure indicated in guideline No. (i) only if,
having regard to the age, fiscal background and strata of the society to which the claimant belongs and such other considerations, the Tribunal thinks that in the larger interest of the claimant and with a view to ensure the safety of the compensation awarded, it is necessary to invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit. 
Thus, sufficient discretion has been given to the Tribunal not to insist on investment of the compensation amount in long term fixed deposit and to release even the whole amount in the case of literate persons. However, the Tribunals are often taking a very rigid stand and are mechanically ordering in almost all cases that the amount of compensation shall be invested in long term fixed deposit. They are taking such a rigid and mechanical approach without understanding and appreciating the distinction drawn by this Court in the case of minors, illiterate claimants and widows and in the case of semiliterate and literate persons. It needs to be clarified that the above guidelines were issued by this Court only to safeguard the interests of the claimants, particularly the minors, illiterates and others whose amounts are sought to be withdrawn on some fictitious grounds. The guidelines were not to be understood to mean that the Tribunals were to take a rigid stand while considering an application seeking release of the money. 
The guidelines cast a responsibility on the Tribunals to pass MACT No. 677/19 Binod Das vs.
Devansh Gupta Page no. 18 of 21 BK appropriate orders after examining each case on its own merits. 
However, it is seen that even in cases when there is no possibility or chance of the feed being frittered away by the beneficiary owing to ignorance, illiteracy or susceptibility to exploitation,
